templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. While updating {record|the}, you realize an entry you made earlier today is wrong. No one has noticed. Your workplace requires corrections to be dated and initialed rather than erased.[[twist]]

twists.text: The next shift starts in ten minutes.
Your {lead} is in a meeting down the hall.

templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Mark the correction with the date and your initials, then tell your {lead} what changed.
options.why: A marked correction keeps the record's history visible, and telling your {lead} lets others keep trusting the information in it.

options.text: Leave it alone, since no one has noticed and the difference is small.
options.why: Even small errors carry forward into decisions and reports. Accurate records depend on each person fixing mistakes they find, whether or not anyone has noticed.
options.misconception: Small mistakes that nobody notices do not matter.

options.text: Erase the wrong entry and write in the right one so {record|the} looks clean and tidy.
options.why: Erasing hides that a change happened, which makes the record harder to trust or check. The workplace rule asks for a visible, dated correction.
options.misconception: A clean-looking record is the same as an honest one.

options.text: Wait for your {lead} to review {record|the} and correct it only if it gets flagged.
options.why: Waiting leaves a known error in place and pushes your responsibility onto a reviewer who may not catch it. You found the mistake, so correct it promptly.
options.misconception: Fixing a mistake is the reviewer's job, not mine.

templates.principle: Accurate records are a shared responsibility: correct your own errors openly and promptly, using the method your workplace sets.

review.notes: Policy on marked corrections is stated in the scenario. No legal claims. Distractors reflect common beliefs (small errors do not matter; neat equals honest; reviewers will catch it).

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You knock into the {equipment} hard and hear a loud crack. It still seems to work. {coworker} is scheduled to use it in about ten minutes, and your {lead} is across the building but can be reached by phone.
templates.timing: Another person will use possibly damaged equipment within minutes, so the first action must disclose the damage and prevent that use.

options.text: Tell your {lead} what happened right away, and warn {coworker} not to use the {equipment} until it is checked.
options.why: Telling the person in charge immediately lets the damage be assessed before anyone relies on the {equipment}. Owning the mistake quickly also protects your coworker.

options.text: Test the {equipment} yourself first to see whether it is really damaged, then decide whether to report it.
options.why: Testing possibly damaged equipment can make the damage worse or put someone at risk, and it delays telling the person who decides what happens next.
options.misconception: I should only report a problem once I am sure it is serious.

options.text: Say nothing for now and see whether {coworker} has any trouble when {coworker} uses it.
options.why: Using someone else as the test puts them at risk and hides your part in the problem. A crack you heard is a reason to speak up even if nothing looks wrong.
options.misconception: If nothing visibly goes wrong, no one needs to know.

options.text: Jot a note about the knock for the end of your shift so that it is documented.
options.why: Documenting it later does not stop the equipment from being used in the meantime. Written notes matter, but a possible hazard needs a spoken report right now.
options.misconception: Writing it down later counts the same as reporting it.

templates.principle: Own a mistake as soon as you notice it, especially when others may rely on what you damaged. Report first, document after.

review.notes: No operation of equipment is suggested; best action is report and keep others from using it. Generic equipment, no specialized knowledge needed. Timing is explicit (ten minutes).

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Client|a} asks you directly whether {deliverable|the} will be ready tomorrow. Your {lead} told you this morning that it needs about two more days. You would like to avoid disappointing {client|a}.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Say honestly that it will not be ready tomorrow, explain that it needs more time, and offer to keep them updated.
options.why: Giving accurate information lets the person plan around the real date. Being honest about a delay protects trust more than a hopeful answer that turns out wrong.

options.text: Say it will be ready tomorrow, since there is a chance it might still get finished early and nobody would be upset.
options.why: Promising a date you do not expect to meet misleads the person, and they may make plans based on it.
options.misconception: A hopeful answer is kinder than an honest delay.

options.text: Give a vague answer that sounds positive without mentioning a date.
options.why: A deliberately vague answer still leaves a false impression. The person asked a direct question and deserves a direct answer.
options.misconception: Not lying outright means I am being honest.

options.text: Ask the person to check back later and let someone else share the delay.
options.why: Passing the news to someone else avoids an uncomfortable moment but leaves the person without the information you already have.
options.misconception: Bad news is better coming from someone else.

templates.principle: Give accurate information, even when it disappoints; honest answers let others plan and keep their trust.

review.notes: Delay confirmed by the lead in the scenario; no legal claims.

templates.scenario: You receive this chat message from a coworker.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that is a problem.

segments.whyFine: A greeting and a heads-up carry no problem.

segments.text: I forgot about an appointment, so I need to leave at 2:00.
segments.whyFine: Needing to leave early is an ordinary situation that can be handled openly.

segments.text: Can you clock me out at 4:00 so it looks like I worked the whole shift?
segments.why: Asking someone to record hours that were not worked is dishonest and puts both people at risk. An honest request would be to arrange an early departure with the supervisor.

segments.text: I will cover your closing task next week to say thanks.
segments.whyFine: Offering to return a favor is friendly on its own; the problem is what the favor is.

templates.principle: Time records must show the hours actually worked. If you need time away, arrange it openly rather than asking someone to cover it up.

review.notes: Falsifying a time record is dishonest regardless of workplace; no unstated policy needed.

templates.scenario: While working at {workplace|the}, you find a wallet on a chair. Your workplace's procedure says found property must be written down, and returned only as your {lead} directs.
templates.prompt: Put these steps in the order you would follow the procedure.

steps.text: Keep the wallet somewhere safe so it is not lost
Tell your {lead} what you found and where
Write down what was found, when and where
Follow your {lead}'s instructions for returning it

precedence.why: Keeping it safe comes first, so it is still there when you report it.
Returning is done as your lead instructs, which comes after telling them.
The record should exist before the item leaves your care.
You should secure the item before spending time on paperwork.

templates.principle: Handle found property by securing it, reporting it, recording it, and returning it as instructed.

review.notes: Procedure stated in scenario; no legal claims.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. Your {lead} asks you to write the expected figure on {record|the} rather than what you actually found, which is a little different, saying a correction would only mean extra paperwork. A written agreement your workplace signed requires accurate records.

options.text: Record what you actually found, explain the difference to your {lead}, and ask how to handle the extra paperwork.
options.why: The agreement requires accurate records, so writing a figure you know is wrong would break it. Raising it with your {lead} openly keeps the record honest and the paperwork manageable.

options.text: Write the expected figure and add a note saying what you actually found.
options.why: The note is honest, but the entry is still wrong, and the agreement asks for accurate records. The record itself should show the true figure.
options.misconception: A note makes a wrong number acceptable.

options.text: Write the expected figure as asked, since your {lead} is responsible for what goes on the record.
options.why: Following an instruction does not remove your responsibility for what you write, especially when an agreement requires accurate records.
options.misconception: I am not responsible if my supervisor told me to.

options.text: Leave the entry blank and say nothing, so that no figure ends up on the record at all.
options.why: A blank entry avoids the question but leaves the record incomplete, and your {lead} still does not know what you found.
options.misconception: Not entering anything keeps me out of trouble.

templates.principle: Report accurate information when a rule requires it, and raise concerns openly instead of entering a number you know is wrong.

review.notes: Requirement stated as a written agreement in the scenario; no jurisdiction-specific legal claims.
